items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the arrangement of taxa in ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species"?
items.answer: Taxonomic hierarchy
items.markingKey: Taxonomic hierarchy: the arrangement of taxa in ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.stem: Explain why viruses are not included in the three-domain classification.
items.answer: Viruses are non-cellular; they have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or metabolism and can only reproduce inside host cells, so they do not fit the features of any domain.
items.markingKey: non-cellular [1]; no metabolism / ribosomes / only reproduce in host [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the three-domain system replaced the five-kingdom system.
items.answer: Molecular evidence (rRNA sequences, membrane lipids, RNA polymerase) showed that prokaryotes form two very different groups, Bacteria and Archaea, which are as different from each other as from eukaryotes.
items.markingKey: molecular / rRNA evidence [1]; two prokaryote groups very different [1] [2]

items.stem: The classification of the domestic dog is: Eukarya, Animalia, ?, Mammalia, Carnivora, Canidae, Canis, familiaris. Which taxonomic rank is missing?
items.answer: Phylum
items.markingKey: Order: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; missing rank = phylum (Chordata).

items.stem: The taxa to which the honeybee belongs are given in random order: Animalia, Eukarya, Insecta, Apis, Apidae, Arthropoda, Hymenoptera, mellifera. Arrange them in order from domain to species, naming each rank, and write the scientific name correctly.
items.answer: domain: Eukarya; kingdom: Animalia; phylum: Arthropoda; class: Insecta; order: Hymenoptera; family: Apidae; genus: Apis; species: mellifera. Scientific name: Apis mellifera.
items.markingKey: correct order [2]; ranks named [1]; binomial written with capital genus and lower-case species [1] [4]

items.stem: Scientists in Cape Town are classifying organisms isolated from a hot spring, together with a virus, the smallpox virus, which contains double-stranded DNA. (a) Explain how the smallpox virus is classified. (b) Describe the features of the kingdom Protoctista.
items.answer: (a) By its nucleic acid: double-stranded DNA; and other features (large, complex); viruses are not placed in a domain because they are non-cellular. (b) Eukaryotic; mostly single-celled (some multicellular algae); some photosynthetic (plant-like), some heterotrophic (animal-like); diverse group not fitting other kingdoms.
items.markingKey: (a) nucleic acid type and strandedness [1]; not in domains [1] [2] (b) eukaryotic [1]; diverse features [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct order of taxonomic ranks, from largest to smallest?
options: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, domain, phylum, order, class, family, genus, species
Domain, phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, genus, species
Domain, kingdom, class, phylum, order, family, species, genus
items.answer: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
items.markingKey: Use a mnemonic for D K P C O F G S.

items.stem: Which feature is found in Bacteria but not in Archaea?
items.answer: Peptidoglycan in the cell wall
items.markingKey: Archaeal walls lack peptidoglycan.

items.stem: An organism has 70S ribosomes, no nucleus and cell membranes containing ether-linked lipids. In which domain is it classified?
items.answer: Archaea
items.markingKey: Ether-linked lipids are characteristic of Archaea.

items.stem: Compare the features of the kingdoms Fungi and Plantae.
items.answer: Both eukaryotic with cell walls. Fungi: chitin walls, heterotrophic, no chloroplasts, hyphae, glycogen store. Plants: cellulose walls, autotrophic with chloroplasts, starch store.
items.markingKey: cell wall composition [1]; nutrition [1]; storage carbohydrate / body form [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain the advantages of using scientific (binomial) names.
items.answer: Each species has a unique name used internationally, avoiding confusion from local common names; the genus name shows close relationships.
items.markingKey: universal / unique [1]; shows relationship [1] [2]

items.stem: A newly described organism is a prokaryote with peptidoglycan cell walls and ester-linked membrane lipids. To which group does it belong?
items.answer: Bacteria
items.markingKey: Bacteria.

items.stem: Diego examined a multicellular heterotroph whose cells have no cell walls and which has a nervous system. State, with reasons, the domain (and kingdom, if appropriate) in which it should be classified.
items.answer: Eukarya (kingdom Animalia): features given match this group.
items.markingKey: correct group [1]; two features used as reasons [2] [3]

items.stem: Describe the three-domain system of classification and the features of the four eukaryotic kingdoms.
items.answer: Domains Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya with distinguishing features (walls, lipids, rRNA, ribosomes, histones); Eukarya kingdoms: Protoctista, Fungi (chitin, heterotrophic, hyphae), Plantae (cellulose, chloroplasts, autotrophic), Animalia (no wall, heterotrophic, nervous coordination); hierarchy; viruses separate.
items.markingKey: three domains with features [3]; four kingdoms [3]; hierarchy / viruses [1] [7]

items.stem: Scientists in Dubai are classifying organisms isolated from a hot spring, together with a virus, the smallpox virus, which contains double-stranded DNA. (a) Explain how they would decide whether a prokaryote isolated from the hot spring belongs to the Bacteria or the Archaea. (b) Explain how the smallpox virus is classified.
items.answer: (a) Test the cell wall for peptidoglycan; analyse membrane lipids (ether vs ester bonds); sequence rRNA genes and compare; examine RNA polymerase. (b) By its nucleic acid: double-stranded DNA; and other features (large, complex); viruses are not placed in a domain because they are non-cellular.
items.markingKey: (a) cell wall [1]; membrane lipids [1]; rRNA sequencing [1] [3] (b) nucleic acid type and strandedness [1]; not in domains [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "mark-release-recapture"?
options: The variety of ecosystems, habitats, species and genetic diversity within species in an area.
A relationship between two variables; it does not prove that one causes the other.
A method of estimating the population size of mobile animals using the Lincoln index: N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂.
The number of different species present in an area.
items.answer: A method of estimating the population size of mobile animals using the Lincoln index: N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂.
items.markingKey: Mark-release-recapture: a method of estimating the population size of mobile animals using the Lincoln index: N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂.

items.stem: Explain why biodiversity is important.
items.answer: Ecosystem stability and services (pollination, nutrient cycling, water purification); sources of food, medicines and genes for crops; economic (tourism); ethical / aesthetic reasons.
items.markingKey: any 3 from: Ecosystem stability and services (pollination, nutrient cycling, water purification); sources of food, medicines and genes for crops; economic (tourism); ethical / aesthetic reasons (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between species richness and biodiversity measured with Simpson's index.
items.answer: Richness counts species only; Simpson's index also accounts for evenness (relative abundance), so two areas with the same richness can have different diversity.
items.markingKey: richness = number of species [1]; Simpson's includes evenness [1] [2]

items.stem: Amara sampled a grazed pasture in Cape Town using ten randomly placed 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats. Total numbers of each plant species: yarrow 34, self-heal 3, ryegrass 40. Calculate the mean density of the most common species per m², given that ten quadrats were used.
items.answer: 16 per m²

items.stem: Noah sampled a road verge in Cape Town using ten randomly placed 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats. Total numbers of each plant species: ryegrass 18, yarrow 37, buttercup 18, daisy 10, dandelion 36. (a) State what the value of D indicates about the biodiversity of the area. (b) Describe how the quadrats were placed randomly.
items.answer: (a) Fairly high biodiversity: D is close to 1, so species richness and evenness are high. (b) Lay two tape measures at right angles as axes; use a random number generator to give coordinates; place the quadrat at each coordinate.
items.markingKey: (a) correct interpretation linked to value [1] (b) grid / axes [1]; random number coordinates [1] [2]

items.stem: Ethan sampled a grazed pasture in Cape Town using ten randomly placed 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats. Total numbers of each plant species: ryegrass 28, dandelion 24, yarrow 22, clover 13, self-heal 27, buttercup 26. (a) Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)². (b) State what the value of D indicates about the biodiversity of the area.
items.answer: (a) 0.826 (b) Fairly high biodiversity: D is close to 1, so species richness and evenness are high.

items.stem: Jonas used a belt transect from inside a woodland to an open field in Doha. At 5 m intervals, light intensity (lux) and percentage cover of grass were: 0 m: 11816 lux, 94%; 5 m: 10278 lux, 85%; 10 m: 10247 lux, 82%; 15 m: 9962 lux, 84%; 20 m: 6542 lux, 58%; 25 m: 2478 lux, 27%. (a) Describe how the percentage cover of grass in a quadrat would be estimated. (b) Suggest two other abiotic factors that could change along the transect.
items.answer: (a) Use a 1 m² quadrat divided into 100 squares; count the squares more than half covered by grass, or use a point frame; each square = 1%. (b) Soil moisture; soil pH; temperature; humidity; mineral ion concentration; leaf litter depth.
items.markingKey: (a) grid quadrat [1]; counting method [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: Soil moisture; soil pH; temperature; humidity; mineral ion concentration; leaf litter depth (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Ravi used a belt transect from inside a woodland to an open field in Lisbon. At 5 m intervals, light intensity (lux) and percentage cover of grass were: 0 m: 11625 lux, 93%; 5 m: 11150 lux, 90%; 10 m: 10710 lux, 88%; 15 m: 8048 lux, 65%; 20 m: 4851 lux, 32%; 25 m: 3780 lux, 28%. (a) Describe the relationship between light intensity and grass cover. (b) Name a statistical test to find whether the correlation is significant, and state why it is suitable. (c) Explain why a belt transect was used rather than random sampling.
items.answer: (a) Grass cover is higher where light intensity is higher (positive correlation). (b) Spearman's rank correlation; the data are paired measurements that may not be normally distributed. (c) There is a gradient of conditions from woodland to field; a transect samples systematically along it, showing how distribution changes.
items.markingKey: (a) Grass cover is higher where light intensity is higher (positive correlation) [1] (b) test [1]; reason [1] [2] (c) There is a gradient of conditions from woodland to field [1]; a transect samples systematically along it, showing how distribution changes [1] [2]

items.stem: Why are quadrats placed at coordinates from a random number generator?
options: To avoid bias in choosing sampling sites
To sample only the most diverse areas
To ensure all quadrats contain the same species
items.answer: To avoid bias in choosing sampling sites
items.markingKey: Every point has an equal chance of selection.

items.stem: Give the meaning of the term belt transect.
items.answer: A line across a habitat along which quadrats are placed at regular intervals, used to study changes in distribution.
items.markingKey: A line across a habitat along which quadrats are placed at regular intervals, used to study changes in distribution. Main idea [1] + precise detail [1] [2]

items.stem: Two meadows each contain the same five species. Meadow X has a higher Simpson's index than meadow Y. What does this show?
options: X has more species than Y
Y has a dominant species absent from X
X has fewer individuals than Y
Individuals in X are spread more evenly among the species
items.answer: Individuals in X are spread more evenly among the species
items.markingKey: Same richness; higher evenness.

items.stem: 30 snails are marked and released; later 40 are caught, of which 6 are marked. What is the estimated population?
Explain why systematic sampling along a transect is used instead of random sampling in some studies.
items.answer: Where there is an environmental gradient (e.g. shore, woodland edge), a transect shows how distribution changes with the gradient; random sampling might miss zones.
items.markingKey: environmental gradient [1]; shows change in distribution [1] [2]

items.stem: Zara caught 60 ground beetles in a garden in Cairo, marked each with a dot of non-toxic paint and released them. Two days later 50 were caught, of which 17 were marked. State two assumptions made in this estimate.
items.answer: No births/deaths or migration between samples; marks not lost and do not affect survival or behaviour; marked animals mix randomly.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: No births/deaths or migration between samples; marks not lost and do not affect survival or behaviour; marked animals mix randomly (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Lina sampled a grazed pasture in Singapore using ten randomly placed 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats. Total numbers of each plant species: thistle 13, dandelion 21, daisy 13, clover 20. Calculate the mean density of the most common species per m², given that ten quadrats were used.
items.answer: 8.4 per m²

items.stem: Ines caught 50 snails in a garden in Karachi, marked each with a dot of non-toxic paint and released them. Two days later 40 were caught, of which 8 were marked. Estimate the population size using the Lincoln index.

Yusuf caught 40 woodlice in a garden in Kuala Lumpur, marked each with a dot of non-toxic paint and released them. Two days later 50 were caught, of which 3 were marked. (a) Estimate the population size using the Lincoln index. (b) State two assumptions made in this estimate.
items.answer: (a) 667 (b) No births/deaths or migration between samples; marks not lost and do not affect survival or behaviour; marked animals mix randomly.

items.stem: Zara sampled a school field in Seoul using ten randomly placed 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats. Total numbers of each plant species: dandelion 28, thistle 22, self-heal 27, clover 22, ryegrass 10, yarrow 2. (a) State what the value of D indicates about the biodiversity of the area. (b) Describe how the quadrats were placed randomly. (c) Calculate the mean density of the most common species per m², given that ten quadrats were used.
items.answer: (a) Fairly high biodiversity: D is close to 1, so species richness and evenness are high. (b) Lay two tape measures at right angles as axes; use a random number generator to give coordinates; place the quadrat at each coordinate. (c) 11.2 per m²
items.markingKey: (a) correct interpretation linked to value [1] (b) grid / axes [1]; random number coordinates [1] [2] (c) area sampled = 10 × 0.25 = 2.5 m² [1]; 28 ÷ 2.5 = 11.2 per m² [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how you would investigate whether the distribution of a plant species is correlated with soil moisture across a habitat, and how you would analyse your results.
items.answer: Belt transect across gradient; quadrats at regular intervals; percentage cover / density; measure soil moisture (dry mass method or probe); repeat transects; plot scatter graph; Spearman's rank: null hypothesis, ranks, d², formula, compare critical value at p = 0.05; correlation not causation; Pearson's if normally distributed.
items.markingKey: sampling method [2]; measuring abundance [1]; measuring moisture [1]; statistical test [2]; limitation [1] [7]

(a) Name a statistical test to find whether the correlation is significant, and state why it is suitable. (b) Explain why a belt transect was used rather than random sampling. (c) Suggest how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Spearman's rank correlation; the data are paired measurements that may not be normally distributed. (b) There is a gradient of conditions from woodland to field; a transect samples systematically along it, showing how distribution changes. (c) Repeat the transect several times at different places; take light readings at the same time of day / repeated; use more quadrats.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "endangered species"?
options: A species at risk of extinction because its numbers are low or falling.
The breeding of endangered animals in zoos to increase their numbers, often for later reintroduction.
The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species: an international agreement that regulates or bans trade in endangered species and their products.
A facility where seeds are dried and stored at low temperature to conserve the genetic diversity of plants.
items.answer: A species at risk of extinction because its numbers are low or falling.
items.markingKey: Endangered species: a species at risk of extinction because its numbers are low or falling.

items.stem: Explain why small populations of endangered species are at greater risk of extinction.
items.answer: Low genetic diversity (founder effect, drift, inbreeding) reduces ability to adapt to change or disease; chance events can wipe out the population; inbreeding depression lowers fertility.
items.markingKey: low genetic diversity [1]; inbreeding / drift [1]; vulnerable to disease / chance events [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how assisted reproduction (IVF, embryo transfer, surrogacy) helps conservation.
items.answer: Gametes/embryos can be frozen and transported instead of animals; more offspring from valuable females via superovulation; surrogate mothers of related species; increases genetic diversity by using unrelated donors.
items.markingKey: freezing / transport of gametes [1]; more offspring [1]; surrogacy / genetic diversity [1] [3]

items.stem: Surveys show that the population of the Sumatran orangutan fell from 13,000 in 1990 to 1,500 in 2020. Suggest two likely causes of this decline.
items.answer: Habitat loss (deforestation, agriculture); poaching / illegal trade; climate change; pollution; by-catch.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Habitat loss (deforestation, agriculture); poaching / illegal trade; climate change; pollution; by-catch (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Surveys show that the population of the hawksbill turtle (nesting females) fell from 45,000 in 1980 to 13,500 in 2020. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in the population. (b) Calculate the mean decrease in population per year.
items.answer: (a) 70% (b) 788 per year

items.stem: Conservationists are working to save the Wollemi pine, which was discovered in 2000 with fewer than 100 trees in the wild; seeds and cuttings are now grown in botanic gardens and seed banks. (a) Explain why captive breeding programmes keep studbooks of all individuals. (b) Explain the role of international agreements such as CITES in conserving this species.
items.answer: (a) To choose breeding pairs that are not closely related, maximising genetic diversity and avoiding inbreeding depression. (b) Ban or regulate trade in the species and its products, reducing incentives for poaching or collection.
items.markingKey: (a) To choose breeding pairs that are not closely related [1]; maximising genetic diversity and avoiding inbreeding depression [1] [2] (b) Ban or regulate trade in the species and its products [1]; reducing incentives for poaching or collection [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the main reason that seeds are dried before storage in a seed bank?
options: To prevent germination and reduce damage to cells when frozen
To make them lighter to transport
items.answer: To prevent germination and reduce damage to cells when frozen
items.markingKey: Low water content and low temperature keep seeds viable for decades.

items.stem: Why are frozen embryos used in captive breeding programmes?
options: They can be stored and transported easily to increase genetic diversity in other populations
They avoid the need for surrogate mothers
items.answer: They can be stored and transported easily to increase genetic diversity in other populations
items.markingKey: Frozen zoo.

items.stem: Explain why it is important to preserve genetic diversity in seed banks as well as in protected areas.
items.answer: Seed banks store many alleles (e.g. from wild relatives and landraces) safely ex situ; protection against loss of habitat; source of genes for future crop breeding and reintroduction.
items.markingKey: store alleles / diversity [1]; insurance against loss [1]; future breeding [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why controlling an invasive alien species can help conserve native species.
items.answer: Removing the alien reduces competition, predation or disease affecting native species, so their populations can recover.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Removing the alien reduces competition; predation or disease affecting native species; so their populations can recover (1 mark each) [2]

items.answer: (a) 218 per year (b) Protected areas / national parks with anti-poaching patrols; CITES trade ban; captive breeding and reintroduction; habitat restoration and corridors; education.

items.stem: Discuss the threats to biodiversity and the methods used to conserve endangered species.
items.answer: Threats: habitat loss, overexploitation, pollution, climate change, alien species. Conservation: protected areas (national parks, marine reserves), zoos and captive breeding, assisted reproduction (IVF, embryo transfer, surrogacy, frozen zoos), seed banks, botanic gardens, CITES, controlling alien species, restoring degraded habitats; problems: cost, genetic diversity, reintroduction.
items.markingKey: threats [2]; in situ methods [1]; zoos / captive breeding [1]; assisted reproduction [1]; seed banks [1]; CITES / alien control [1] [7]

items.stem: Conservationists are working to save the giant panda, which lives in fragmented bamboo forests in China and breeds very slowly in captivity. (a) Explain the advantages of conserving a species in its natural habitat compared with in a zoo or botanic garden. (b) Explain why captive breeding programmes keep studbooks of all individuals.
items.answer: (a) In situ: the whole ecosystem and its interactions are protected; natural behaviour and selection continue; larger populations; cheaper per individual. (b) To choose breeding pairs that are not closely related, maximising genetic diversity and avoiding inbreeding depression.
items.markingKey: (a) ecosystem protected [1]; natural behaviour / selection [1]; larger population [1] [3] (b) To choose breeding pairs that are not closely related [1]; maximising genetic diversity and avoiding inbreeding depression [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Lima states: "Keeping a few individuals of a species in a zoo is enough to save it from extinction." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Small captive populations lose genetic diversity; breeding programmes need many unrelated individuals and habitat protection for reintroduction.

items.stem: Surveys show that the population of the hawksbill turtle (nesting females) fell from 52,000 in 1990 to 16,700 in 2020. Describe two ways in which the species could be conserved.
items.answer: Protected areas / national parks with anti-poaching patrols; CITES trade ban; captive breeding and reintroduction; habitat restoration and corridors; education.

items.stem: Surveys show that the population of the Bornean orangutan fell from 160,000 in 1995 to 65,500 in 2025. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in the population. (b) Calculate the mean decrease in population per year.
items.answer: (a) 59.1% (b) 3150 per year

items.stem: Conservationists are working to save the giant panda, which lives in fragmented bamboo forests in China and breeds very slowly in captivity. (a) Explain the advantages of conserving a species in its natural habitat compared with in a zoo or botanic garden. (b) Discuss the problems of reintroducing captive-bred animals to the wild.
items.answer: (a) In situ: the whole ecosystem and its interactions are protected; natural behaviour and selection continue; larger populations; cheaper per individual. (b) Lack of survival skills (hunting, predator avoidance); habitat may still be degraded; disease; low genetic diversity; local people's attitudes.

items.stem: Scientists in Istanbul are classifying organisms isolated from a hot spring, together with a virus, the measles virus, which contains single-stranded RNA. (a) Explain how the measles virus is classified. (b) Describe the features of the kingdom Protoctista.
items.answer: (a) By its nucleic acid: single-stranded RNA; and other features (enveloped); viruses are not placed in a domain because they are non-cellular. (b) Eukaryotic; mostly single-celled (some multicellular algae); some photosynthetic (plant-like), some heterotrophic (animal-like); diverse group not fitting other kingdoms.

items.stem: Nadia used a belt transect from inside a woodland to an open field in Toronto. At 5 m intervals, light intensity (lux) and percentage cover of grass were: 0 m: 3066 lux, 25%; 5 m: 3503 lux, 31%; 10 m: 3618 lux, 24%; 15 m: 7545 lux, 62%; 20 m: 8100 lux, 57%; 25 m: 10261 lux, 73%. (a) Describe how the percentage cover of grass in a quadrat would be estimated. (b) Describe the relationship between light intensity and grass cover. (c) Explain why a belt transect was used rather than random sampling. (d) Suggest how the reliability of the results could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Use a 1 m² quadrat divided into 100 squares; count the squares more than half covered by grass, or use a point frame; each square = 1%. (b) Grass cover is higher where light intensity is higher (positive correlation). (c) There is a gradient of conditions from woodland to field; a transect samples systematically along it, showing how distribution changes. (d) Repeat the transect several times at different places; take light readings at the same time of day / repeated; use more quadrats.
items.markingKey: (a) grid quadrat [1]; counting method [1] [2] (b) Grass cover is higher where light intensity is higher (positive correlation) [1] (c) There is a gradient of conditions from woodland to field [1]; a transect samples systematically along it, showing how distribution changes [1] [2] (d) any 2 from: Repeat the transect several times at different places; take light readings at the same time of day / repeated; use more quadrats (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Hana used a belt transect from inside a woodland to an open field in Dhaka. At 5 m intervals, light intensity (lux) and percentage cover of grass were: 0 m: 11366 lux, 85%; 5 m: 7795 lux, 67%; 10 m: 7262 lux, 62%; 15 m: 3698 lux, 31%; 20 m: 3612 lux, 35%; 25 m: 1336 lux, 12%. (a) Describe the relationship between light intensity and grass cover. (b) Name a statistical test to find whether the correlation is significant, and state why it is suitable. (c) Explain why a belt transect was used rather than random sampling.
items.answer: (a) Grass cover is higher where light intensity is higher (positive correlation). (b) Spearman's rank correlation; the data are paired measurements that may not be normally distributed. (c) There is a gradient of conditions from woodland to field; a transect samples systematically along it, showing how distribution changes.
